html:
The fruit of a woody vine native to China, which was brought to New Zealand in 1904 and grown there into a world export crop. It was renamed kiwifruit for export in 1959.

The seeds were carried from the mission town of Yichang in central China, then under the Qing, by Mary Isabel Fraser, head of a girls' school in Whanganui. A local nurseryman, Alexander Allison, grew the first vines that bore fruit, in about 1910. New Zealanders called it the Chinese gooseberry. In the 1920s the grower Hayward Wright bred the large, sweet Hayward variety that still dominates the trade.

New Zealand began to export the fruit in the 1950s. Because of the Cold War and import rules in the United States, exporters wanted a new name, and in 1959 the firm Turners and Growers chose kiwifruit, after New Zealand's national bird. The fruit is now grown in Italy, Chile, Greece and above all China, the world's largest producer. See New Zealand and the farm export trade that began with the first frozen meat shipment.
sum: The fruit of a woody vine native to China, which was brought to New Zealand in 1904 and grown there into a world export crop. It was renamed kiwifruit for export in 1959.
